keyVerseText: I have digged and drunk strange waters, and with the sole of my feet have I dried up all the rivers of besieged places. besieged: or, fenced
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun מָצוֹר (mâtsôwr) fundamentally conveys the idea of a place under siege or a fortified stronghold. Its root sense encompasses both the physical reality of an enclosure or defense system—such as a bulwark, tower, or entrenchment—and the abstract notion of being hemmed in or under distress. This root meaning enriches the English glosses by emphasizing not just a static location but the dynamic condition of protection or siege, highlighting the tension between vulnerability and security.
usageInScripture: The word מָצוֹר occurs four times in Scripture with translations ranging from 'besieged places' to 'defence' and 'fortified.' This variety shows a consistent semantic field centered on protection, enclosure, and siege, whether referring to physical locations under attack or metaphorical fortifications. The fact that it also serves as a poetic name for Egypt underscores its use as a boundary or stronghold in a broader territorial sense, illustrating the word's flexibility within a framework of defense and enclosure.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מָצוֹר in its original sense deepens our appreciation of God as both refuge and sovereign defender of His people. The imagery of siege and fortified places reminds believers that spiritual life often involves being surrounded by trials or enemies, yet God provides a secure stronghold. This word invites reflection on divine protection amid adversity, encouraging faith in God's power to preserve and sustain. It also points to the biblical motif of God as a fortress, reinforcing trust in His unassailable defense against spiritual and temporal threats.
keyVerseReflection: In 2 Kings 19:24, the phrase 'I have digged and drunk strange waters, and with the sole of my feet have I dried up all the rivers of besieged places' uses מָצוֹר to evoke the desperation and encirclement experienced under siege. The term 'besieged' here, alternatively rendered as 'fenced,' highlights the confinement and pressure faced by those trapped. This word enriches the verse by emphasizing the tangible reality of being hemmed in, underscoring the severity of the situation and the miraculous nature of God's intervention in such desperate circumstances.
